title: Hausa cities: walls, markets and kings
intro: Walled towns grew across the Hausa lands of today's northern Nigeria. This chapter begins with Kano. Most of its early dates come from the Kano Chronicle, a history compiled from older traditions. It counts reigns by their length, so its years are a later reckoning and are labelled that way. The copy translated in 1908 was written down in the late nineteenth century; the historian Murray Last argues its first edition dates from the mid-1600s.

features.name: Kano · walled city
features.what: Kano grew around Dala hill. By the Kano Chronicle's reckoning its first wall was begun between 1095 and 1134, and Muhammad Rumfa (1463–1499) built a palace, extended the walls through named gates and founded Kurmi market. The palace site, Gidan Rumfa, is still the emir's residence, and Kurmi still trades.
features.evidence: The Kano Chronicle (compiled from older traditions; Palmer's 1908 translation), Nigeria's 2007 heritage file, archaeology cited by Iliffe, and architectural history
features.location: Representative point for the old walled city, rounded; not a survey of the walls or gates.

monument.note: Original schematic stage set of an earth-built city, not a survey or reconstruction. Each part appears at its own date (listed under What appears when). The Chronicle names the gates but does not place them, so gate positions, wall lines, the palace footprint and the market are schematic; the walls are drawn as sun-dried earth (tubali) on a sloping profile with a crenellated crest. Nothing later is added: no present-day palace decoration (mostly 1930s–40s), no 1951 mosque or minaret, no 16th-century wall line, no emblem or bridge.

features.name: Kano · the people inside
features.what: Who lived in Kano in the fifteenth century, told from the Kano Chronicle's reigns of Abdullahi Burja (1438–1452), Yakubu (1452–1463) and Muhammad Rumfa (1463–1499), by its reckoning, and from Leo Africanus's description, written in 1526.

features.location: Representative point for the old walled city, rounded; not a survey of the walls or gates.

features.name: Katsina
features.what: Another Hausa city, north-west of Kano, with its own king. Its rulers moved here in the fifteenth century from Durbi ta Kusheyi, and Muhammadu Korau, its first Muslim king, is credited with founding the walled town. The Kano Chronicle records that Kano's first war with Katsina came in Rumfa's reign and lasted eleven years, with neither side winning.
features.location: Today's city centre, rounded. The fifteenth-century town's extent is not drawn, and the earlier seat at Durbi ta Kusheyi, about 29 km to the south-east, is not placed.
features.label: left

features.name: Bornu
features.what: The kingdom east of Kano that grew from Kanem. By the Kano Chronicle's reckoning, Abdullahi Burja (1438–1452) was the first Hausa king to send it tribute, and he opened the road from Bornu to Gwanja through Kano.
features.location: Drawn at Ngazargamu, which became Bornu's capital about 1472. The point stands for the kingdom, not a city.

features.name: Daura
features.what: Remembered in Hausa tradition as the mother city of the Hausa states: there, the story says, Bayajidda killed the snake in the Kusugu well and married Queen Daurama. By one historian's reading, tribute to Bornu was sent by way of Daura.
features.location: Today's town of the same name.

features.name: Kano
features.what: Kano as one Hausa state among several, each with its own king. Its Chronicle supplies most of this chapter's dates, so Kano's view of its neighbours is the one best recorded.

features.name: Zazzau
features.what: The southern Hausa state. Captives taken in the lands to its south were collected there and sent north to the markets of Kano and Katsina. Its best-known figure, Amina, is dated differently by different sources.
features.evidence: Secondary sources, and the Kano Chronicle on Amina
features.location: Drawn at today's Zaria, which was founded about 1536. Zazzau's earlier capitals, such as Turunku, are not placed: the dashed ring marks the region, not a site.

features.name: Gobir
features.what: The northernmost Hausa state, which tradition gives the task of war against invaders. Under Tuareg pressure from the north its people moved south more than once.
features.location: Drawn at today's Birni Lalle in Niger, inside a wide ring, because where Gobir's capital stood in these years is uncertain.
features.disputed: One summary makes Birnin Lalle Gobir's capital from about 1450 to 1600, but the same article's text dates the move there to the early eighteenth century, and earlier centres in Asben or at Marandet are also proposed.

features.name: Rano
features.what: One of the seven Hausa states of tradition. By the Kano Chronicle's reckoning Kano's king Yaji (1349–1385) drove out its king, and Rano never regained its independence, so it is drawn faintly.
features.location: Today's town of the same name.

features.name: Biram
features.what: The seventh Hausa state of tradition, founded by Bayajidda's son by a princess of Bornu. One historian counts it, with Kano, among the states that paid tribute to Bornu.
features.location: Drawn at today's Hadejia, which was once known as Biram. The old town of Biram itself is not placed: the dashed ring marks the area.

features.name: Kebbi
features.what: A Hausa-speaking state to the west, which tradition lists among the Banza Bakwai, seven states it ranked below the Hausa seven. In 1516 its leader Kanta rebelled against Songhai and defeated the army sent against him.
features.evidence: Secondary sources, resting partly on the Tarikh al-Sudan
features.location: Drawn at Surame, the walled town Kanta built in the sixteenth century, to stand for Kebbi. His first capital, Birnin Leka, is not placed.

features.name: Kano's tribute to Bornu
features.what: By the Kano Chronicle's reckoning, Abdullahi Burja (1438–1452) was the first Hausa king to send tribute to Bornu.

features.name: Biram's tribute to Bornu
features.what: The historian M. G. Smith counted Biram, with Kano, among the Hausa states that paid tribute to Bornu, sent by way of Daura.
features.disputed: Whether every Hausa state paid tribute to Bornu, or only Kano and Biram, is unclear, and how long they paid is not known.

scenes.title: The earth becomes a city

when.label: About 1000–1499 · archaeology and the Kano Chronicle

scenes.text: Before Kano was a city, it was a hill. People worked iron on Dala. The Kano Chronicle remembers Barbushe, keeper of a shrine on the hill. That memory is tradition, and it has no date. By the Chronicle's reckoning, King Gijimasu began a wall, gate by gate. Who finished it? The Chronicle says Yusa, in the 1100s. Nigeria's heritage file says Zamnagawa, in the 1300s. Then Muhammad Rumfa. The Chronicle says he built a palace and moved in the next year. The year after, he pushed the walls outward, gate by gate. He founded a market, Kurmi, which still trades today. A scholar, al-Maghili, wrote Rumfa a book on how a king should rule. A walled city needs more than walls. Who lived inside them?
scenes.disputed: Who finished Kano's first wall? The Kano Chronicle credits Yusa (1136–1194 by its reckoning); Nigeria's 2007 UNESCO tentative-list file credits Zamnagawa, in the mid-14th century. The age of the Dala settlement also differs: the 7th century (Iliffe) or the 10th (UNESCO file).

scenes.title: Who lived inside the walls

when.label: 1438–1526 · Kano Chronicle reckoning and Leo Africanus

scenes.text: Go back before Rumfa, to King Abdullahi Burja. People already lived inside the first wall. The Chronicle says Burja opened roads from Bornu, in the east, to Gwanja, in the south-west. He was the first in Hausaland to own camels. He was also the first to send tribute to Bornu. His men raided the south for captives, and settled them in twenty-one new towns. Under Yakubu, Fulani came from Mali with books on divinity and etymology. Salt became common in Hausaland. Then came Rumfa: his palace, new walls through named gates, and Kurmi market. Traders and scholars came to the city. Rumfa gave offices of state to eunuchs, and began a council of nine, the Tara-ta-Kano. He began kulle, the seclusion of women, and was the first to have kakaki, long royal trumpets. In his time came Kano's first war with Katsina. It lasted eleven years, and neither side won. Writing in 1526, Leo Africanus described Kano's people as wealthy merchants and skilled craftsmen. Whether he ever went there is doubted. By then, Wangara merchants had probably brought kola nuts into the trade.
scenes.disputed: Did Leo Africanus see Kano? Fisher (1978) doubts that he visited Hausaland at all, so his description is given as his account, not as an eyewitness record. Yakubu's reign is 1452–1463 by the Chronicle's eleven years; one summary starts it in 1432.

scenes.title: Hausa cities side by side

when.label: 1349–1516 · Kano Chronicle reckoning and other sources

scenes.text: Hausa tradition tells of Bayajidda, a prince from the east. At Daura he killed the snake that guarded the well, and married the queen. Their descendants, the story says, founded seven Hausa states. They were never one kingdom: each walled city had its own king, the sarki. In the story each had its task. Kano and Rano dyed cloth with indigo, Katsina and Daura kept the markets, Gobir fought off invaders, and Zazzau supplied slaves. The cities fought each other. Kano's king Yaji drove out the king of Rano, and Rano never ruled itself again. The Chronicle says that in Dauda's reign Zazzau, under Queen Amina, conquered the towns as far as Kwararafa and Nupe. Other sources place her a century or more later. Kano's Abdullahi Burja was the first Hausa king to send tribute to Bornu. Whether every city paid, or only Kano and Biram, is not known. In Katsina, a cleric, Muhammadu Korau, became the first Muslim king. He is credited with the walled town that grew into Katsina city. Kano and Katsina, the two great markets, fought for eleven years in Rumfa's reign, and neither side won. Then Songhai's armies came from the west. Askia Muhammad attacked Katsina; how far Songhai ruled the Hausa cities is disputed. In 1516 Kanta of Kebbi broke with Songhai and beat the army sent against him. The Hausa cities stayed separate until the jihad of 1804.

scenes.disputed: Amina's dates differ by more than a century: the Kano Chronicle puts her in Dauda's reign (1421–1438), a Zaria list in the early sixteenth century, and others after 1576; her name is missing from Zazzau's king lists, and whether she was queen is disputed. Korau of Katsina is dated about 1445–1495 by the Katsina Chronicle, 1492–1541 by another list and to the thirteenth century by a local tradition. Songhai's hold on the Hausa cities is disputed: one account dates Askia's conquest of Katsina to 1512 and has Katsina a vassal until 1554, others say he also took Zazzau and Gobir, and Leo Africanus, whose visit is doubted, adds Kano.
